concepts.heading: You Are Not Broken
concepts.plain: Many people with long-term conditions have satisfying sex lives, often in new ways.

concepts.heading: Grief Is Normal
concepts.plain: It is OK to miss what sex used to be like before you build something new.

concepts.heading: Look Beyond One Kind of Sex
concepts.plain: Intimacy can include touch, massage, oral sex, toys, kissing and closeness.

checks.prompt: Since her diagnosis, Lee feels sad that sex isn't what it was. What does this lesson suggest?
options: She should stop thinking about sex
Missing how things were is normal, and naming it can help her adapt
She should hide it from her partner
checks.explanation: Grief over what has changed is natural. Naming it is often the first step to finding new ways to be close.

fe4905b6-6c57-52c5-ab66-13a7856f5d49.takeaway: Health changes call for adapting intimacy, not giving it up.

concepts.heading: Budget Your Energy
concepts.plain: Plan intimacy for times you have energy, not the end of a draining day.

concepts.heading: Time It With Your Treatment
concepts.plain: Some people feel best at certain times after medicine or treatment.

concepts.heading: Set Up for Comfort
concepts.plain: Pillows, wedges, warmth and positions that need less effort can make a big difference.

concepts.heading: Pace Yourself
concepts.plain: Shorter sessions and breaks are fine. Stop before pain builds.

checks.prompt: Ravi's pain is lowest mid-morning. How could he use that?
options: Change his medicine timing without telling his doctor
Only have sex late at night when he's exhausted
Plan intimate time for mornings when he feels better
checks.explanation: Planning around the times you feel best is a simple, effective adjustment. Talk to a clinician before changing medicine timing.

fd70080b-2864-5c28-adf8-923f64cf41f1.takeaway: Plan around your good times, set yourself up for comfort, and pace yourself.

concepts.heading: When Care Crowds Out Romance
concepts.plain: Helping with medical care can make it hard to see each other as lovers.

concepts.heading: Keep Some Time Just for You Two
concepts.plain: Set aside time that is about connection, not care tasks.

concepts.heading: Look After the Caregiver Too
concepts.plain: Caregivers burn out. Their rest and support matter too.

concepts.heading: Many Partners, Shared Care
concepts.plain: In larger families or networks, care and intimacy can be shared out openly.

checks.after: Keep Some Time Just for You Two
checks.prompt: Kim helps her partner with daily care and no longer feels romantic. What might help?
options: Doing even more care tasks to show love
Setting aside time for connection that has no care tasks in it
checks.explanation: Separating care time from partner time helps both people feel like partners again.

00113e66-bfce-5b4c-bea5-05986eab0619.takeaway: Keep caregiving and partnership separate, and look after both people.

concepts.heading: Sex Is a Health Topic
concepts.plain: Your sexual health deserves the same care as any other part of your health.

concepts.heading: Ask About Side Effects
concepts.plain: Many medicines affect desire, arousal or orgasm. There are often alternatives.

concepts.heading: Bring Questions
concepts.plain: Writing questions down makes awkward topics easier to raise.

concepts.heading: Keep Asking
concepts.plain: If one clinician brushes you off, it is fine to ask someone else.

checks.prompt: Jordan's new medicine has lowered his desire. What should he do?
options: Tell his clinician and ask about other options
checks.explanation: Stopping some medicines suddenly is dangerous. Talking to a clinician opens up safe options.

1b9f050b-ddcd-594a-b541-ef5b436dffa6.takeaway: Sex is a health topic. Ask, and keep asking until you get help.
